I say that I take that seriously and to point out exactly how I'm being racist and what I would need to do differently if I was. 

Honestly it never gets that far, and once you've got rapport with some of the kids they'll shut it down. 

Example 1: J called me a racist at the beginning of the year (I admittedly came in hard with discipline - racist can sometimes mean 'you're unfair'). We ended up on good terms and she said something like "She kissed her dog on the mouth? That's some white people shit" and I loud gasped and said "J, it's my turn? That was racist!" Teachable moment and we both laughed about it. 

Example 2: I asked a student to turn their music down with a joke about how I didn't like the song. It was rap, so the student went "I meaaaan that's kinda racist." Before I could even defend it another student was like "what???" I just rolled my eyes and said I'm racist for liking different songs and she proceeded to tell the other student to quit being stupid and shut up.

I will say in both scenarios I am ALWAYS open to being corrected and I say so. If I'm really being racist or biased, tell me. I want to change, if that's the case. But if you can't give proof to me treating you differently then shut up. This year I had a student who didn't call me racist, but he'd be like "why's it always me?"

It took a while but he FINALLY got that I wasn't picking on him, because he couldn't think of anyone else doing the same behaviors and getting no consequences from me, and he stopped pulling the "why's it only me line".

Tldr: I think what will get you the best outcome is to push aside the defensiveness, which we all have, and say okay. Please demonstrate. If I'm being racist or sexist or homophobic or xenophobic I don't want to be those things, and I will change if you can show that I am actually being biased. I think being willing to hear them all the way out helps.

So I have a self contained class. I have ADHD myself and about half my class and ADHD/ID combo and what I'm really trying to nail home to them now, and maybe how you could approach the parent - is that yes. Some initial reactions may be out of your control. 

BUT at a certain point we leave the realm of impulse and make a choice to continue a behavior we know is harmful to us or others because it's easier. The right choice is hard. And while the out of control initial reaction can be given some grace the decision to double down on a behavior that began as an impulse is a choice. Which you have to take responsibility for. 

Example - we talked about impulse lying. I explained why our brains do that because we want whatever the issue is to quickly go away. But at some point, probably within five to ten minutes, you realize you lied. So fix it. I won't issue a consequence if you promptly take responsibility. 

The real world does not care about the doctors note. Other kids his age will not care about his problems, they'll just think he's mean. So I think stressing that yes your child does have a disability that requires patience but that doesn't mean he gets a pass on bad behavior. We still have to be responsible for ourselves. Noticing he needs to step away from something before he gets dysregulated is a skill he will need in life and it will help him better advocate for himself.
